title: Recovering a burnt server from backups and config in git
summary: A RAID controller caught fire while I was debugging a power supply. Infrastructure as code and off-cluster backups brought the platform back in about four hours, and I wrote down every mistake.

stat.label: to rebuild the main platform from code and backups, not days

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: The server had a power-supply warning light. It had two supplies, so I pulled them one at a time to find the bad one. When I tested the bad one, the RAID controller caught fire.

On 3 September both nodes of my two-node cluster dropped within the same second, and every guest followed within moments. The router and a separate GPU machine stayed up, which ruled out a power event on the circuit and a network fault. The fault light and the smell of burning pointed at the controller. The second node was collateral: it lost the media share the first one served.

sections.heading: What I built before it happened
paragraphs: Backups that did not live in the cluster they protected. Every guest had a recent archive on a directory store attached to the GPU machine, which is bare metal and never went down. Backups written to the cluster would have burned with it.
The nightly backup had finished between 02:30 and 03:01 that morning, so the newest archive was only hours old when the fire started.

sections.heading: Recovery
paragraphs: The surviving node came up without quorum, so its configuration store was read-only and nothing could start. I set the expected vote count to one, removed the dead member, and cleared its node directory to free the guest IDs. Before the last step I copied every guest config off the dead node, because they were the only record of how each guest was wired. They now live in git.

Archives existed for every guest. I restored them from the archives onto the surviving node and flashed a fresh machine as a new third node, and Terraform and Ansible brought the main services back in about four hours. The smaller services came back over the next couple of days, because I used the outage to decide which ones I still needed. I no longer run a container registry, for example. The platform tier moved onto the new node: a dozen containers in under an hour, with no data loss and no rebuild.

Terraform could not move a container, because a changed node name forces replacement. The plan gates refused the change and showed red CI, which was the gate working. I reconciled state with a repair script scoped to one environment, and I now reach for declarative state blocks first, wherever the language can express the repair.

sections.heading: What I lost
paragraphs: The media library. The disks sat behind a hardware RAID controller with a controller-specific on-disk format, and the controller was the part that burned. I cannot read those disks in another machine.
The rebuild uses ZFS on plain disks, so any machine with the disks attached can import the pool. Hardware RAID made the data hostage to one card.

sections.heading: What went wrong during recovery
paragraphs: Four mistakes, three of them mine. The rescued configs named a storage pool that only existed on the dead node. The network bridge had a different name on the surviving node. My remap loop checked only the first network interface, so one guest with a second interface came up with no network. And an empty result from a privileged command nearly became the report that no backups existed.

After the hypervisor was back, the applications were not usable. The downloader reported a space error that was a missing directory. The media managers still held records for files that died with the array, and one request app pointed at a server that no longer existed. Nothing warns you that a downstream service moved; the requests just fail.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: The fire was my mistake. I tested a failing power supply on a live server with a hardware RAID controller in it, and I lost the media because only that controller could read the disks. I own that.

The better choices are the ones I made afterward: ZFS on plain disks that any machine can import, backups outside the failure domain, and guest config in git. An empty result is not evidence of an empty directory, so I check the exit status before I report absence.

The old GPU machine later became a cluster node itself, so the cluster is back to three nodes. I wrote the incident up while the detail was fresh, and every mistake became a check in the migration guide.

sources: Pedro's account in the case-study thread, 2026-11-03 (power-supply sequence, about four hours)
